ground_truth_root_cause: A BGP route leak from upstream transit provider AS64501 injected a more-specific prefix (203.0.113.32/27) for the payment processor IP range (canonical route: 203.0.113.0/24 via AS64502). Because BGP prefers longer prefixes, all outbound traffic to payment processor IP 203.0.113.45 was redirected to AS64501, which black-holed the traffic rather than forwarding it. This caused 100% packet loss to the payment endpoint for 8 minutes (14:03-14:11 UTC). The leak is evidenced in the logs by: the bgp-monitor alert at 14:04:25Z identifying the AS64501 more-specific prefix advertisement, the network-probe traceroute at 14:03:40Z showing traffic dying at the AS64501 boundary, and the recovery confirmation at 14:11:03Z after AS64501 withdrew the leaked route.
ground_truth_remediation: 1. Contact AS64501 NOC immediately to request withdrawal of leaked prefix 203.0.113.32/27 (NOC was already engaged by 14:09:30Z). 2. Apply BGP prefix filters on the peering session with AS64501 to reject prefixes more-specific than /24 for IP ranges not owned by AS64501, preventing future leaks from this peer. 3. As short-term mitigation during future incidents: configure a static route or policy-based routing to force payment processor traffic via the secondary ISP link, bypassing the affected transit peer. 4. Escalate BGP route anomaly alerts to PagerDuty with auto-page to NOC to reduce time-to-engage. 5. Coordinate with the payment processor to retry or reprocess all failed orders from the 14:03-14:11 UTC window and notify affected customers.
red_herring: The Kubernetes HPA config update (SHA f62a8e15d3b90c1, deployed at 13:37 UTC, 25 minutes before the incident) looks suspicious because: (a) it raises the frontend scale-up CPU threshold from 60% to 80%, and an engineer might hypothesize that this caused the frontend to under-scale under load, creating backpressure that cascaded into checkout payment timeouts; the temporal proximity and infrastructure-level scope make it a plausible first suspect. However, the logs contain clear exculpatory evidence: (1) at 14:05:01Z the HPA controller logs show frontend CPU at only 43%, well below even the old 60% threshold, meaning no scale-up was suppressed and no frontend saturation occurred; (2) at 14:06:10Z checkout-service logs explicitly note that all 5 checkout pods report identical ETIMEDOUT errors to the same destination IP, ruling out any pod-count or frontend issue; (3) the errors are TCP connect timeouts to a specific IP (203.0.113.45:443), not HTTP 5xx or application-layer errors consistent with compute saturation; (4) DNS and TLS are confirmed healthy at 14:04:18Z and 14:04:19Z respectively; (5) full recovery at 14:11:14Z occurs with no HPA or deployment change, solely after BGP route withdrawal by AS64501, definitively excluding the HPA deploy as a contributing cause.
